primitives.name: Forward Reinforcement Gradient
primitives.verbatim_quote: Thorndike and his associates have reported evidence which suggests that the gradient of reinforcement may extend also in the forward direction; i.e., that learning may be reinforced when the reinforcing state of affairs precedes the S - R conjunction as well as when it follows it.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'t_f': 'time interval (seconds), forward delay from reinforcement to behavior'}
primitives.assumptions: Reinforcement history influences future learning; temporal precedence of reward affects behavioral conditioning strength.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When t_f exceeds critical threshold, gradient diminishes below detectable levels.

layer2.mapping: Maps prior reinforcement timing to current learning efficacy in GSI; defines temporal kernel for predictive behavioral modeling in GSE.
layer2.telemetry: Behavioral consistency under varying pre-reward intervals

primitives.name: Backward Reinforcement Gradient
primitives.verbatim_quote: Thorndike and his associates have reported evidence which suggests that the gradient of reinforcement may extend also in the forward direction; i.e., that learning may be reinforced when the reinforcing state of affairs precedes the S - R conjunction as well as when it follows it.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'t_b': 'time interval (seconds), backward delay from behavior to reward'}
primitives.assumptions: Post-behavioral reward strengthens association more effectively than pre-behavioral reward.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When t_b approaches zero, gradient becomes undefined due to causality inversion.

layer2.mapping: Encodes post-reward feedback into learning dynamics in GSI; enables dynamic value estimation in GSE.
layer2.telemetry: Learning curve steepness after reward delivery

primitives.name: Yoshioka Path Discrimination
primitives.verbatim_quote: Yoshioka's Study of Path-Length Discrimination in Rats A number of years ago, Yoshioka (17) investigated experimentally the relative difficulty of setting up a consistent preference for the shorter of two paths to a food goal.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'P_{short}(t)': 'probability of selecting short path at time t', 't': 'time (seconds)', 'α': 'normalization constant (dimensionless)', 'β': 'decay rate (s⁻¹)'}
primitives.assumptions: Path preference formation follows exponential decay model; maze size does not significantly alter learning efficiency.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At large t, P_short(t) → 0, indicating loss of preference discrimination.

layer2.mapping: Maps path selection behavior to reinforcement learning kernels in GSI; translates into GSE spatial-temporal decision trees.
layer2.telemetry: Consistency of path choice across mazes of differing sizes

reasoning_traces.think:
The delay-of-reinforcement gradient operates in both directions—forward and backward—whereby the forward gradient reflects anticipation of reward before behavior, while the backward gradient reflects reinforcement following behavior. The forward gradient is less pronounced, suggesting its role in learning is secondary compared to the backward gradient. This duality implies a dual temporal structure in reinforcement learning: one where reward precedes action (predictive), and another where reward follows action (retrospective). In GSI, these gradients inform probabilistic models of behavior prediction, where the backward gradient contributes more heavily to posterior updates. In GSE, they define state transition probabilities in decision-making frameworks. The exponential nature of the path discrimination model (as per Yoshioka) supports a continuous-time stochastic process underlying path selection. The failure mode occurs when either gradient collapses—either due to excessive delay or lack of reinforcement—leading to non-convergence in learning algorithms.
